claims.text: The starting material is commercially available submicron ZrB2 powder.
ZrB2 can be SPS-processed at approximately 1950 °C under approximately 50 MPa in vacuum, using a heating rate of approximately 100 °C/min and a 5–10 minute dwell.
SPS lowers the required ZrB2 preparation temperature from above 2300 °C to approximately 1950 °C.
Fast heating and a short hold at approximately 1950 °C provide minimal thermal exposure while achieving high densification.
SPS at the proposed conditions produces a denser, nearly pore-free ZrB2 microstructure.
The electrical current and mechanical pressure used in SPS create localized Joule heating and rapid mass transport.
Localized heating and rapid mass transport refine the ZrB2 grain structure and eliminate residual porosity.
Spark-induced local heating and applied pressure accelerate ZrB2 densification while minimizing grain growth and porosity.
Reduced porosity and a uniform, dense ZrB2 matrix impede liquid-phase penetration during plating-bath exposure.
Impeded liquid penetration reduces degradation, hole formation, and subsequent component failure during prolonged plating-bath exposure.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will have greater mechanical strength than conventionally prepared ZrB2 sintered above 2300 °C.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will have improved long-term stability in corrosive liquid plating environments relative to conventionally prepared ZrB2.
Conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2 sintered above 2300 °C typically has higher porosity and more microstructural defects.
The greater porosity and defect content of conventionally prepared ZrB2 cause reduced strength and durability in liquid plating baths.
The relevant preparation comparison is SPS near 1950 °C versus conventional processing above 2300 °C.
The relevant service regime is prolonged operation in a liquid plating bath where corrosion, degradation, and hole formation can occur.
